c.tagline: Honduras's mountain-cradled capital of colonial plazas and modern grit.

taxi.color: no uniform color; radio-dispatch cooperatives use varied paint schemes
taxi.fareNote: Taxis are unmetered; agree on a flat fare before departure. Radio-dispatched or hotel-arranged taxis are safer than hailing on the street.

emergency.note: 911 is the national emergency line, dispatching police, fire, and ambulance services throughout Tegucigalpa.

hood_landmark.Lomas del Guijarro: Boulevard Morazán, Colonia Lomas del Guijarro, Tegucigalpa

avoid.reason: High crime; avoid Comayagüela and outskirts, especially at night

hood_desc: Tegucigalpa's leafy diplomatic quarter of embassies, government offices, and tree-lined streets; a safe, central, walkable base favored by business travelers and first-time visitors.
An upscale hillside residential district of gated homes, boutique hotels, and view restaurants above the city; suits travelers wanting quiet, secure lodging a short drive from downtown.
The city's modern commercial spine, lined with malls, chain business hotels, and international restaurants; ideal for visitors who want convenience, reliable Wi-Fi, and easy taxi/rideshare access.

The old heart of the capital on both banks of the Choluteca: the colonial grid of Tegucigalpa proper around the San Miguel cathedral, and Comayagüela on the west bank with its sprawling street markets. Cheap and atmospheric, best for budget travelers and history buffs comfortable with a grittier streetscape by day.
A trendy pocket of cafes, bars, and the Los Próceres park popular with young professionals and expats; a good mid-range base close to nightlife and casual dining.
lodging: InterContinental Tegucigalpa at Multiplaza Mall by IHG

water.note: Avoid tap water; stick to bottled or purified water.

transit.pay: Fares on city buses and colectivos are paid in cash (lempiras) directly to the driver or fare collector; there is no widespread rechargeable transit card yet. The Trans450 BRT, being rolled out in stages, is introducing prepaid card readers at its dedicated stations.
transit.hours: Most public buses run roughly 5:30am-8pm; service is sparse and unreliable after dark, so taxis or rideshare are the norm at night.
transit.note: Tegucigalpa's steep terrain, narrow colonial streets, and heavy traffic make public buses slow and confusing for visitors; most tourists rely on taxis, hotel transport, or Uber rather than city buses.

air: Toncontín International Airport (TGU), Tegucigalpa - domestic and regional flights only since international service relocated to Palmerola
bus: Intercity coaches (Hedman Alas, Viana, El Rey) to San Pedro Sula, Comayagua, and other cities from private terminals

airport.name: Palmerola International Airport (XPL)
airport.drive: 1.5-2 hours via CA-5 highway (mountainous two-lane road; longer in rain or heavy traffic)

tip.r: Tipping isn't obligatory. Many restaurants already add a 10% service charge (propina), in which case extra tipping isn't expected; round up for taxis and casual services.

food.name: Baleadas
food.desc: Honduras' national snack: a thick soft flour tortilla folded over refried beans, salty cheese and crema. Con todo adds egg, avocado and meat.

places.name: El Patio
places.note: Long-running institution for Honduran classics; the standard baleada many locals judge others by.

places.name: Baleadas Express
places.note: Honduran chain built entirely on baleadas; quick, cheap and consistently good fillings.

places.name: The Market
places.note: Popular modern restaurant serving baleadas alongside other Honduran staples.

food.name: Plato tipico
food.desc: The full Honduran plate: grilled carne asada with chismol salsa, fried plantain, refried beans, fresh cheese, mantequilla crema and tortillas.

places.name: El Patio
places.note: Famous grill house where the plato tipico arrives on a sizzling platter; a Tegucigalpa rite.

places.name: Duncan Maya
places.note: Old-school Honduran restaurant near the centre, popular for typical plates at lunch.

places.name: La Cumbre
places.note: Hillside restaurant with city views serving generous typical plates and grilled meats.

food.name: Anafre
food.desc: Honduran bean and cheese fondue kept bubbling over coals in a clay pot, scooped up with crisp tortilla chips. The classic thing to share.

places.name: El Patio
places.note: Serves anafre in the traditional clay burner as a starter for the table.

places.name: The Market
places.note: Reliable anafre alongside a broad Honduran and international menu.

places.name: La Cumbre
places.note: Good place to share anafre and drinks with a view over Tegucigalpa at dusk.

food.name: Tajadas con pollo
food.desc: Green plantain fried into crisp slices, piled with shredded cabbage salad, chicken or chorizo, and squirted with salsa rosada. Honduran fast food at its best.

places.name: Mercado Los Dolores food stalls
places.note: Downtown market comedores frying tajadas to order for a few lempiras.

places.name: Baleadas Express
places.note: Does tajadas and other quick Honduran plates alongside the baleadas.

places.name: El Patio
places.note: Sit-down version with grilled chicken, generous portions and table service.

food.name: Sopa de caracol
food.desc: Caribbean conch soup from the north coast, simmered with coconut milk, yuca, green plantain and culantro. Rich, fragrant and famously restorative.

places.name: The Market
places.note: Regularly cited for its sopa de caracol, one of the easiest places in the capital to find it.

places.name: El Patio
places.note: Keeps coastal Honduran dishes including conch soup on the traditional menu.

places.name: La Cumbre
places.note: Weekend menus often feature coastal soups and fish alongside the grill.

food.name: Nacatamales and pastelitos
food.desc: Corn-dough nacatamales steamed in banana leaf with pork and rice, and pastelitos de carne, crisp fried corn turnovers eaten with cabbage and salsa.

places.name: Mercado Los Dolores food stalls
places.note: Market cooks sell nacatamales and pastelitos from early morning, especially at weekends.

places.name: Mercado San Isidro
places.note: Huge working market with comedores turning out tamales and fried snacks all day.

places.name: Duncan Maya
places.note: Sit-down option for tamales and other Honduran comfort food near the old centre.

food.name: Honduran coffee
food.desc: Honduras is Central America's biggest coffee producer; look for single-origin beans from Marcala, Copan and Santa Barbara, served black or as a cortado.

places.name: Espresso Americano
places.note: Honduran-owned chain that made local coffee everyday drinking; found on most main streets.

places.name: Cafe Honore
places.note: Specialty roaster and cafe pouring single-origin Honduran lots for the coffee-serious.

places.name: Cafe Paradiso
places.note: Bookshop-cafe and cultural hangout downtown, a calm spot for a cup and a pastry.

food.name: Horchata
food.desc: Honduran horchata is made from ground morro seeds, rice and spices rather than almonds, served cold and cloudy with lunch.

places.name: Mercado Los Dolores food stalls
places.note: Market refresco stands ladle horchata and other fresh drinks from glass jars.

places.name: El Patio
places.note: Serves horchata and other traditional refrescos with the typical plates.

places.name: Mercado San Isidro
places.note: Comedor counters pour horchata, tamarindo and chan by the glass.

landmarks: Basílica de Suyapa
This grand neo-Gothic basilica houses the tiny revered statue of the Virgin of Suyapa, Honduras's patron saint, drawing massive pilgrimages every February.
Metropolitan Cathedral of San Miguel Arcángel
Facing the historic central plaza, this 18th-century colonial cathedral with an ornate gilded Baroque altar is the spiritual heart of Tegucigalpa's old town.
Cristo del Picacho
A towering white statue of Christ perched atop El Picacho hill offers sweeping panoramic views over the entire capital, much like Rio's famous counterpart.
Teatro Nacional Manuel Bonilla
This elegant early 20th-century neoclassical theater remains the nation's premier venue for opera, ballet, and concerts behind an ornate historic facade.
Iglesia Los Dolores
One of the city's oldest churches, this striking colonial-era temple with twin bell towers anchors a charming plaza in the historic downtown.
Antigua Casa Presidencial
The former seat of Honduran government, this stately early 20th-century building now hosts cultural exhibits and photogenic colonial architecture downtown.
Museo para la Identidad Nacional (MIN)
Housed in a beautifully restored former palace, this leading museum traces Honduran history and culture from Maya civilization to the present day.
Parque Central (Plaza Morazán)
The lively main square, framed by the cathedral and colonial buildings, centers on a statue of national hero Francisco Morazán and buzzes with daily life.
Estadio Nacional Chelato Uclés
Honduras's largest football stadium electrifies visitors on match days, serving as the passionate home ground for the national team and top clubs.
Río Choluteca and City Skyline
The river winding through the capital offers classic photo vantage points of Tegucigalpa's hillside skyline sprawling across the surrounding mountains.

train.note: Honduras has no intercity passenger railway (the only surviving rail is a short tourist line on the north coast). Travel is by coach or car.

intl.to: San Salvador, Guatemala City, Managua, San José & Panama City (+ Tapachula, Mexico)
San Pedro Sula, Copán & Guatemala City (Guatemala)

bus.note: Tica Bus is the workhorse for cross-border coaches, linking Tegucigalpa to every Central American capital and on to Tapachula, Mexico. Carry your passport for the border crossings.

ferry.note: Tegucigalpa is inland with no ferry service. Honduras's passenger ferries run on the Caribbean coast (La Ceiba to the Bay Islands of Roatán and Utila) and are domestic only.

full.name: Managua
full.blurb: Nicaragua's lakeside capital, known for its volcanoes and mix of old and new landmarks.

full.name: San Salvador
full.blurb: El Salvador's capital, a volcano-ringed city with a lively historic center.

full.name: San Pedro Sula
full.blurb: Honduras's industrial hub, known as a gateway to Caribbean coast and Maya sites.

full.name: Soyapango
full.blurb: Densely populated city near San Salvador known as a key industrial and commercial hub.

full.name: Santa Ana
full.blurb: Salvadoran city known for its striking theater and nearby volcano and coffee farms.

full.name: Mejicanos
full.blurb: Densely populated San Salvador suburb known for its lively markets and everyday urban life.

full.name: León
full.blurb: Historic Nicaraguan city known for colonial churches, colorful streets, and revolutionary murals.

full.name: Choloma
full.blurb: Honduran industrial city known for its manufacturing and growing population.
